key_insight: Early three-dimensional vorticity growth in transonic shock–boundary-layer interactions is dominated by viscous and compressibility effects, while vortex stretching becomes appreciable intermittently with shock-induced separation.
engineering_relevance: Understanding when three-dimensional effects emerge can guide the use of 2D versus 3D simulations when assessing transonic natural-laminar-flow airfoil performance.
method: Run high-fidelity 3D simulations of the SHM1 airfoil across normal-shock onset, drag divergence, and shock-induced separation.
Compare spanwise-averaged 3D pressure and skin friction with previously reported 2D simulations.
Track streamwise and wall-normal enstrophy and analyze the compressible enstrophy transport budget.
evidence_signal: Across three operating conditions, 2D–3D comparisons identify an initial interval of close agreement followed by departures, while normalized enstrophy budgets show regime-dependent redistribution among the same principal mechanisms.
watch_item: The study addresses short-time evolution for one airfoil at three operating conditions, so long-time behavior and broader design generality remain unestablished.
paper_title: Onset of three dimensionality in transonic shock boundary layer interaction over a natural laminar flow airfoil
